title: N matters: Insights into nitrogen assimilation from the ectomycorrhizal fungus Laccaria bicolor
content: Nitrogen (N) is an essential macronutrient for the growth of plants and fungi, yet its availability often limits productivity in forest ecosystems (Paré and Thiffault 2016). Ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi establish mutualistic associations with tree roots, enhancing N acquisition and facilitating its transfer from soil to host plants. ECM fungi do not penetrate root cells but form a branched hyphal network between epidermal and cortical cells of the root, the Hartig net, and a hyphal sheath that covers the root tip, the mantle (Balestrini and Bonfante 2014). This relationship improves plant nutrient status, while the fungus benefits by receiving carbon compounds from the host (Martin et al. 2008). The capacity of ECM fungi to assimilate diverse N sources (ammonium, nitrate, and amino acids) is crucial for their survival and symbiotic function (Stuart and Plett 2019). Laccaria bicolor has become a valuable model for studying the molecular basis of ECM symbiosis (Martin and Selosse 2008). Although L. bicolor can use various N forms, ammonium is preferred due to its lower energetic cost during assimilation (Stuart and Plett 2019). In ammonium-poor forest soils, however, the ability to utilize alternative N forms becomes essential (Martin et al. 2008). Once assimilated, ammonium is incorporated into glutamine (Gln) and glutamate (Glu) via the Gln synthetase (GS)/Glu synthase (GOGAT) cycle or through the NADP-dependent Glu dehydrogenase (NADP-GDH) pathway (Figure). Both pathways function in ECM, with variations depending on the plant and fungal partners (Morel et al. 2006). Yet, the molecular mechanisms that enable L. bicolor to process N and sustain symbiosis remain underexplored.
